old: Mathematics usually publishes a proof after the proof has been compressed. Definitions have stabilized. Failed attempts have disappeared. A long calculation has become a lemma. A representation change that made the argument visible is replaced by a direct sentence. This is often an improvement. The final certificate is easier to verify and easier to reuse.
new: A published proof often presents an argument after its exploratory work has been compressed. Definitions have stabilized, unsuccessful approaches have been set aside, and a long calculation may now appear as a lemma. The change of representation that first made the argument visible can disappear into a single sentence. Such compression is often useful: it leaves a certificate that is easier to check and reuse.

old:
The finite theory developed here has six connected layers.

\begin{enumerate}
\item A typed proof field records claims, admissible leaves, justifications, evidence, and targets.
\item A certified subfield separates proved or otherwise certified transitions from candidates and interpretations.
\item A certificate is a selected subfield that derives the target.
\item Compression is evaluated relative to declared tasks rather than by length alone.
\item A bridge graph represents possible future reach and makes archival retention an optimization problem.
\item Versioning, review, audit, and refinement describe the life of the proof after the first certificate exists.
\end{enumerate}
new:
The construction begins with a typed field of claims, justifications, evidence, and targets. Its certified rules determine which targets are derivable. A certificate selects enough of those records to support a declared conclusion, while the ambient field can retain unresolved or refuted alternatives.

A second layer asks what survives when the field is compressed. The answer depends on the questions that a representation must support. An archive intended for future discovery may preserve examples and failed approaches that a verification certificate can omit. A bridge graph makes one such retention problem precise.

The final layer concerns the continuing life of the archive. Revisions change the set of claims that need review. Shared errors affect the information supplied by multiple reviewers. Audit capacity limits how quickly new candidates can be checked. These models are connected by their declared proof objects, without treating social judgments as substitutes for deduction.

note: The ambient development treats the proof field as an ambient field of candidate and certified paths. It connects coherent local proof views to the str
old: The ambient development treats the proof field as an ambient field of candidate and certified paths. It connects coherent local proof views to the strict Komorebi realization construction, and adds an exact finite information measure for informative observations. The mathematical validity of a proof remains distinct from how communities discover, interpret, or review it.
new: Komorebi Space enters when local descriptions of a proof field must agree. The construction of local rule models supplies actual restriction maps, not merely a visual analogy between two graphs. A gluing theorem identifies a sufficient condition for assembling those models, and a counterexample explains why pairwise dependency checks can miss a conjunctive rule. In a separate linear setting, the size of a realization fiber measures exactly what a new observation distinguishes.

old: The theory is intentionally finite at its foundation. Finite objects make every closure condition and algorithm explicit. Infinite, probabilistic, and higher categorical extensions are listed later as open programs rather than silently assumed.
new: The implemented proof fields are finite and acyclic. Some structural statements, including rule soundness and the linear separation alternative, are given in greater generality where their hypotheses allow it. Extensions to infinite search, probabilistic inference, and higher categorical proof objects require their own assumptions. Background on formal proof systems may be found in \cite{buss,troelstra}.

new: A node is an admissible leaf when it is a required premise, a declared axiom, or an explicitly admitted external result. Write $L$ for this set, so $A\subseteq L$. A certified justification with no premises can also derive a node, but it remains a justification and need not make that node a member of $L$. The distinction matters when extracting the smallest certificate.

Evidence and scope are part of that policy. A certification flag records acceptance: it is not itself a proof that the rule is sound under an intended mathematical interpretation. Let $\Pcal$ be a finite acyclic AND-DAG relative to $T_0$. Put
\[

\]
Then $(K_{\mathrm{core}},H_{\mathrm{core}})$ is a certificate and is the least certificate under componentwise inclusion. In particular it is the unique inclusion-minimal certificate pair for this recorded inference problem.

note: Backward traversal from each target selects the unique justification that can derive it and every premise required by that justification. Repeating th
old:
Backward traversal from each target selects the unique justification that can derive it and every premise required by that justification. Repeating the process terminates because the dependency graph is finite and acyclic. The selected leaves are admissible, and a forward topological pass derives every selected node, so the construction is a certificate.

Let $(K,H)$ be any certificate for the same target set. Each target must be derived. Since it has one certified incoming justification, that justification must lie in $H$, and all of its premises must lie in $K$. Applying the same argument recursively forces every node and justification in the backward ancestry into $(K,H)$. Therefore every certificate contains the constructed core. Uniqueness and minimality follow.
new:
Backward expansion terminates because the dependency graph is finite and acyclic. Every terminal node is either an admissible leaf or the conclusion of the selected justification with no premises. A forward topological pass therefore derives every expanded node. The required premises in $A$ are admissible and are retained even if the target does not use them. Thus the constructed pair is a certificate.

Now let $(K,H)$ be any certificate for the same request. It contains $A\cup T_0$. If a requested or required predecessor node is outside $L$, its derivation must use its unique certified incoming justification. That justification belongs to $H$, and every one of its premises belongs to $K$. Repeating the argument forces all of $\Anc_L(T_0)$ and $H_{\mathrm{core}}$. At nodes in $L$ the argument stops. Hence $K_{\mathrm{core}}\subseteq K$ and $H_{\mathrm{core}}\subseteq H$, which proves the least-pair assertion.

Minimizing one coordinate alone does not make the whole record unique. One may add an irrelevant node without changing the least justification set, or retain an unused rule without changing the least node set. The componentwise statement avoids this ambiguity.

old: The unique core of an AND-DAG can be extracted in time linear in the size of the relevant certified ancestry, assuming indexed adjacency and constant-time membership bookkeeping.
new: With indexed certified adjacency and constant-time membership bookkeeping, the core can be extracted in time linear in $|A|$ plus the number of visited nodes, selected justifications, and premise incidences.

note: Exact minimum certificate search is practical for small fields or fields with few alternatives. Large formal libraries require branch and bound, dynam
old: Exact minimum certificate search is practical for small fields or fields with few alternatives. Large formal libraries require branch and bound, dynamic programming on restricted structures, integer programming, approximation, or proof-system-specific methods. The reference package includes an exact finite search with an explicit state limit. It does not hide the exponential worst case.
new: Exhaustive certificate selection is useful for small fields or fields with few alternatives. The reference implementation uses branch and bound with an explicit search-state limit. Its result is optimal for the stored finite cost data when the search completes. It does not remove the exponential worst case. The decision theorem concerns integer costs, while the Python interface accepts finite floating-point costs and compares their exact stored binary values as rationals. Printed cost totals remain floating-point summaries. The input conversion does not recover an intended real or decimal value that was never represented. See \cite{garey-johnson} for the background complexity language.

note: A certified proof category $\mathsf{Cert}$ has mathematical states as objects and certified transformations as morphisms. Identity morphisms retain a
old: A certified proof category $\mathsf{Cert}$ has mathematical states as objects and certified transformations as morphisms. Identity morphisms retain a state unchanged. Composition is sequential use of compatible certified transformations.
new: Fix a directed graph of typed mathematical states and certified primitive transformations. Its path category $\mathsf{Cert}$ has these states as objects and finite composable paths as morphisms. The empty path is an identity, and composition is concatenation. One may further identify paths by a declared congruence compatible with concatenation. Associativity and the identity laws then hold by construction.

old: The proposition is elementary, but its interpretation is central. A proof may be transported into another language without changing validity. What changes is visibility. A spectral representation may expose a symmetry hidden in physical coordinates. A finite exact computation may expose the correct statement before a general derivation is known. A formal proof assistant may expand dependencies that a journal proof compresses.
new: The proposition transports certification inside the two declared categories. To interpret that transport as preservation of a mathematical judgment, the target category and functor must also have sound interpretations of their objects and rules. These requirements cannot be inferred merely from the word functor. Under that contract, different representations can preserve a judgment while exposing different features of its argument. The category language is standard \cite{maclane}.

note: A representation is not simply good or bad. It is sufficient or insufficient for a declared family of questions.
old: A representation is not simply good or bad. It is sufficient or insufficient for a declared family of questions.
new: A representation is sufficient only relative to specified questions and a specified class of possible archives. Fix a set $\mathscr A$ of admissible proof archives. A representation scheme is a map $C:\mathscr A\to\mathscr R$. Its output for an archive $\Pcal$ is $C(\Pcal)$. Distinguishing the scheme from one output is essential: a decoder chosen only after seeing one fixed archive could simply store the answer.

A task is a map $q:\mathscr A\to Y_q$ to a declared answer set. A task family $\Qcal$ is a set of such maps. Examples include asking for the target certificate, a dependency list, a specified boundary example, or the claims affected by a recorded revision. A teaching or discovery objective becomes an exact task only after its required output or acceptance criterion has been specified.

note: It is easy to speculate that authorship or disciplinary identity changed an evaluation; it is harder to establish such an effect. A direct experimenta
old: It is easy to speculate that authorship or disciplinary identity changed an evaluation; it is harder to establish such an effect. A direct experimental design can hold an argument fixed while randomizing its surrounding label. Let $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ denote the evaluations that a reviewer would give the same declared mathematical content under two different labels. In a randomized design, the difference of treatment-group and control-group mean responses estimates the population average label effect, subject to the usual sampling, assignment, and interference conditions. It does not establish whether the proof is correct. That requires a separate audit of the mathematical claim.
new:
A claim about identity effects needs a design that can distinguish them from other differences. Hold the mathematical content fixed and let $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ be the fixed potential evaluations of reviewer $i$ under two labels. In a finite set of $N$ reviewers, assign exactly $n_1$ to the first label and $n_0=N-n_1$ to the second, uniformly over assignments with those sizes, where $n_0,n_1>0$. Assume each observed response equals the potential response under its assigned label and does not depend on other assignments. Then the difference of the two sample means is unbiased for $N^{-1}\sum_i(Y_i(1)-Y_i(0))$. Indeed, each reviewer has inclusion probability $n_1/N$ in the first mean and $n_0/N$ in the second, so linearity of expectation gives that identity.

This conclusion concerns the assigned reviewers. Generalizing to a broader population requires a sampling model. Missing responses, shared discussion, or changes to the argument itself can invalidate the simple interpretation. None of these comparisons determines whether the proof is correct. Correctness requires its own mathematical audit.
